content.title: Late Filing Penalties: IRS & State Consequences for Missing Tax Deadlines
content.text: Updated Dec 2, 2024, 12:21 PM CT The deadline to pay any individual income tax you owe is April 15. Not filing and paying on time will result in a 5% penalty per month on any unpaid tax and interest. If you file late but don't owe, your refund will be withheld for up to three years until you file. There's usually plenty of time between when you receive all the necessary documents to prepare your tax return and the deadline to submit it.But if you don't think you'll be able to gather the paperwork and file your federal income tax return on time, make sure to file for a tax extension.A tax extension will push your filing due date back six months, but you're still expected to calculate and pay any tax you owe by the due date or set up a payment plan with the IRS.If the April tax deadline comes and goes and the IRS hasn't heard from you at all, you can expect to face a penalty. There's one late charge for not paying what you owe the IRS and another late charge for not filing a return to report what you owe. If you don't do either, the charges can really add up.Failure-to-file penaltyIf you don't file a federal tax return, the IRS will calculate whether you owe money.If you're expecting a tax refund, there's no penalty for late filing — but you won't get your refund until you file. You have three years from the due date of your tax return to file and claim your refund. After that, the money goes back to the U.S. Department of the Treasury.Failure-to-pay penaltyIf you owe money and file your return late, the IRS will charge a combined penalty of 5% of the unpaid tax for each month or part of the month that the balance remains unpaid.When your return is filed more than 60 days after the due date, it's subject to a minimum penalty equal to the lesser of 100% of the tax required to be paid on your return or $485, according to IRS rules. There will also be interest accruing on your balance equal to the federal short-term rate plus 3%.If you haven't paid your bill after five months, the failure-to-file penalty maxes out at 25% of the unpaid tax. The failure-to-pay penalty continues to accrue (0.5% each month) until it hits 25% of the unpaid tax as of the due date.Tax penalty for underpayment of estimated taxesPeople who earn income outside of W-2 work, such as self-employed people, gig economy workers, and certain small business owners, are required to pay estimated taxes on their income at set intervals throughout the year. Keep in mind that some payment apps report to the IRS, too, so you'll need to account for earnings made through Cash App, Venmo, and PayPal.Payments are due on April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15.You can use Form 2210 to determine whether you underpaid and by how much, or wait to receive an IRS notice and bill in the mail.Interest on unpaid taxesThe IRS uses the federal short-term rate (which fluctuates), plus 3%, to determine how much interest you'll owe on your unpaid taxes. The failure-to-pay penalty interest is equal to 0.5% for each month. Note that penalties are calculated on the full amount — the outstanding tax plus interest.Avoiding late filing penaltiesFile an extension If you need more time to file your federal return, it's easy (and free) to get an extension. An extension gives you until October 15 to file, but you must still pay your bill on time or you'll face a failure-to-pay penalty of 0.5% per month on the unpaid tax.You can file for an automatic extension by completing Form 4868 or paying all or part of your tax due through electronic payment. Pay as much as you canIf you didn't pay the amount of income taxes you were supposed to throughout 2024, you may owe the IRS on the April 15 tax deadline. You can use tax software or consult a tax professional to calculate your bill.It's important to report what you owe, if anything, when you file your tax return and pay it — or pay as much as you can — by the deadline.But not everyone has to file taxes. If you made more than the standard deduction for your age and filing status, claimed unemployment income, or were self-employed and had a net income of at least $400 during the year, you must file a tax return with the IRS. Some dependents may be required to file as well.Here are the standard deduction amounts for 2024:Those with a zero or negative tax bill aren't required to file, unless they want to claim refundable credits, such as the earned income tax credit (EITC), or had tax withheld by their employers throughout the year and want to get a refund.Set up a payment planIf the failure-to-pay penalty was charged because you can't afford to pay your bill, contact the IRS as soon as possible. You might be able to set up a payment plan, which is often a better option than paying your bill with a credit card and racking up interest charges.The IRS offers reasonable payment plans at much lower interest rates than most banks. You may even be able to settle the bill for less than you owe, called an offer in compromise, or request a deferment until you can make a payment. Offers in compromise and requests for deferment require additional paperwork and must be approved by the IRS.Request penalty abatementIf you haven't accrued any penalties for failing to file or pay taxes in the past three years, the IRS may agree to forgive your late charges. Other types of penalty relief may be available if you were affected by a serious illness, natural disaster, or other disruptive event.Call the IRS number on the letter you received by mail notifying you of your penalty.Contest the penaltyIf you believe your tax penalty notice was sent in error or the information is incorrect in some way, call the IRS number on the letter you received. But read carefully — some notices include specific instructions and deadlines for disputing a penalty.FAQs on penalties for filing taxes late If you have a valid reason for filing late, or if it's your first tax penalty, penalty relief may be available. This relief could apply if your ability to pay or file on time was impacted by a serious illness, natural disaster, or other disruptive event. Valid reasons for late filing do not include lack of knowledge, reliance on a tax professional, or mistakes and oversights. Yes, you can get an extension to pay your taxes if you can't afford it, but not by filing for a tax extension, which extends your filing date but not your payment date. Instead, you can apply for a payment plan directly with the IRS or ask for a temporary pause on collections. Late filing won't affect your credit score, but it may have an impact on your ability to borrow in the future. If you neglect to pay your back taxes after several notices from the IRS, it could place a federal tax lien on your property. This allows the IRS to seize your assets to satisfy your debt. Federal tax liens are public record and can be used by lenders to evaluate your creditworthiness. Tanza Loudenback is a personal finance expert and a Certified Financial Planner (CFP). She was the founding reporter of Personal Finance Insider, covering topics including taxes, retirement planning, banking, real estate and mortgages, and budgeting. Her work has been featured in WSJ Buy Side, Fortune Recommends, Korn Ferry, TheStreet, Morgan Stanley Wealth Management, and Fidelity. ExperienceTanza was the first reporter on the Personal Finance Insider team. In addition to helping build the vertical from the ground up, she helmed a biweekly advice column answering readers’ personal finance questions and launched a personal finance newsletter. She also published two e-books under the Personal Finance Insider brand.She was the editorial lead on Master Your Money series, a two-year-long Business Insider series providing financial advice to millennials. She managed Master Your Money bootcamp events over the course of the series. While at BI, she also expanded tax coverage to include a guide to the best tax software and commissioned a panel of experts to review all articles. Tanza obtained her CFP license in 2020. She aims to simplify personal finance concepts for readers so that they can make smart decisions with their money.
